title: India Moves to Form Banking Reforms Panel That Could Merge 12 State Banks Into Five
excerpt: The High-Level Committee on Banking for Viksit Bharat is expected to recommend mega-bank consolidation, higher foreign investment caps and NBFC restructuring.
body:
• India's finance ministry is moving to form a High-Level Committee on Banking for Viksit Bharat, first announced in the February 2026 Budget
  • The panel is expected to recommend consolidating 12 public sector banks into five mega-lenders and raising the foreign investment cap to 49%
  • Former Department of Financial Services secretary M. Nagaraju is tipped to head the committee
  • Finance Minister Sitharaman said the 1969 bank nationalisation had "not yielded the desired results" and pushed for "big and world-class banks"

India's government is preparing to constitute a sweeping banking reforms panel that could reshape the country's financial sector for the next two decades, with Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman signaling that the committee will be formed "at the earliest."

The High-Level Committee on Banking for Viksit Bharat — first proposed in the Union Budget on February 1, 2026 — is expected to recommend reducing the number of public sector banks from 12 to approximately five through a fresh round of mergers, while raising the foreign investment cap in state-owned banks from 20% to 49%, according to a Livemint report from June citing finance ministry sources. Former Department of Financial Services secretary M. Nagaraju is tipped to lead the panel.

Sitharaman's Vision for Mega-Lenders

Speaking at the 12th SBI Banking and Economics Conclave, Sitharaman said the government is already in discussions with the Reserve Bank of India and bank heads to chart a roadmap for building "big and world-class banks."

https://x.com/ETNOWlive/status/2089256646455579086

"It is not by creating from those which exist today... just by amalgamation that can also be one of the routes, but you need an ecosystem and an environment in which more banks can operate and operate to grow."

— Nirmala Sitharaman, Finance Minister

In a separate address at the Delhi School of Economics, Sitharaman went further, arguing that the 1969 bank nationalisation had "not yielded the desired results" in terms of financial inclusion. She said government control had made public sector banks "unprofessional" and that fears of losing inclusion objectives through reforms were "incorrect."

At a PTI interview, she framed the panel's mission in broad terms: "We want the committee to tell us what kind of things we need to do so that banking is made available for funding Viksit Bharat. You have to reach Viksit Bharat destination — it needs money, it needs financing, it needs credit, it needs banking facility to reach the common man."

What the Panel Could Recommend

The committee's expected scope goes well beyond mergers. Based on finance ministry signals and expert analysis, the panel is likely to examine:

Bank consolidation: India reduced its public sector banks from 27 to 12 between 2017 and 2020 through a series of mergers — including the absorption of Dena Bank and Vijaya Bank into Bank of Baroda, and five associate banks into State Bank of India. A further round could create five to six mega-lenders with the scale to finance India's infrastructure and industrial ambitions.

Foreign ownership: Raising the foreign investment cap in public sector banks to 49% from the current 20% would attract significant international capital, though the government would retain its controlling 51% stake.

Corporate entry into banking: A 2020 RBI working group recommended allowing corporate houses to set up banks, though the idea faced internal opposition over governance concerns. The committee may revisit this contentious question.

NBFC restructuring: The Budget already proposed restructuring Power Finance Corporation (PFC) and Rural Electrification Corporation (REC). PFC's board has since approved in principle the merger of REC with itself.

Technology and deposits: Banks have struggled with deposit mobilisation as households shift savings to capital markets and new-age investment platforms. The credit-deposit ratio crossed 81%, setting off alarm bells about lending sustainability.

Bank Unions Push Back

Sitharaman's privatisation-friendly comments drew sharp pushback from bank unions and civil society groups. The United Forum of Bank Unions, representing nine trade unions across all banks, pointed out that 90% of accounts under the Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana were opened by public sector banks.

"If Indian banking today stands strong, it is because of resilience built under public ownership... no country in the world has achieved universal banking through privatising banks," the UFBU said in a statement, demanding a categorical assurance that no PSB would be privatised.

NRI Implications

For Non-Resident Indians, the reforms carry both opportunity and caution. Higher foreign investment caps could improve service quality and digital capabilities at state banks, many of which handle NRI deposits and remittances. The RBI's recent FCNR dollar swap scheme has already driven an 86% surge in NRI deposits to 0 billion. But any consolidation wave could also mean branch closures, account migrations and transitional disruptions — particularly for NRIs who rely on specific PSBs for their India banking needs.
